metaDescription: Three 800-watt countertop microwaves compared on sensor cooking, presets, cabinet size and child safety, with honest notes on a thin category.
expertTake: The GE Profile is the best 800-watt pick because sensor cooking offsets the slower heat of the lower wattage. The Nostalgia NRMO9WH is the value choice for a basic, easy-to-clean white unit. Anyone who wants speed should skip this wattage and look at 1000 watts or more.
introParagraphs: Microwaves rated near 800 watts are an in-between size that few makers target. They run a little faster than the 700-watt compact class and a little slower than the common midrange, so the real question is whether the gap buys anything.

Because the field is thin, the honest approach is to judge each model on cavity, controls and safety features rather than on wattage alone. This guide covers the distinct machines that truly carry this rating.

products.name: GE Profile PCHK11S1WSS 1.1 cu ft 800W sensor microwave
products.description:
GE Profile builds this oven around a moisture sensor, and that is what makes the 800 watt output practical. A sensor watches the steam leaving the cavity and ends the cycle when the food is hot, so you are not guessing how much extra time a slower oven needs. At a lower wattage, that automatic judgment is more useful than a longer preset list.

The cavity is 1.1 cubic feet, a step above the 0.9 cubic foot Nostalgia units in this guide, so a standard dinner plate fits with room to spare. One-touch express cooking and four convenience cook settings keep the panel simple, and a child lock protects against stray presses. The stainless finish and Profile styling look at home in a modern kitchen.

Ownership is easy: wipe the interior after steamy foods so the sensor reads correctly, wash the tray by hand and leave a gap behind for airflow. The same unit is sold in black and white versions, so choose a finish by your kitchen rather than by features. Compared with the Nostalgia retro, you pay for sensor logic and a bigger cavity, and you lose the nostalgic look. If the kitchen is shared by several people with different habits, the sensor is the feature that makes the oven forgiving for the least careful user.
products.bestFor: Households that want automatic reheating at a modest wattage and a roomier cavity.
pros: Moisture sensor ends cooking when food is hot
1.1 cu ft cavity fits full dinner plates
Child lock guards against stray presses
Same model in stainless, black and white
cons: 800 W is slower than midrange ovens
Runs pricier than the Nostalgia units

products.name: Nostalgia Retro 0.9 cu ft 800W microwave with 12 presets
products.description:
Nostalgia sells this microwave on looks first and function second, and the retro cabinet is the main reason to choose it. Under the styling is a 0.9 cubic foot cavity, 800 watts of output and twelve pre-programmed cooking settings. A delay timer and express cooking add convenience, and the LED display is easy to read.

The twelve presets cover popular foods like popcorn and pizza, which is a longer list than the GE Profile offers. The tradeoff is that presets are fixed times, so they only fit the food sizes the maker had in mind. There is no sensor to correct for a smaller or larger portion, and 800 watts means you will watch the clock a bit more.

In the kitchen, it behaves like a basic timer-and-power machine. Take a cloth to the interior after use, wash the tray and keep the vents clear on all sides. It suits a game room, a rental or a retro-themed kitchen where the cabinet is part of the decor. Test the presets against a clock the first week and note which ones run short for your portion sizes. Frozen burritos and microwave popcorn bags vary a lot between brands, so the preset names are best seen as shortcuts rather than promises.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a retro-looking microwave with plenty of presets.
pros: Delay timer and express cooking included
LED display is easy to read
cons: 0.9 cu ft cavity is smaller than the GE
Fixed presets suit only standard portions

products.name: Nostalgia NRMO9WH 0.9 cu ft 800W white microwave
products.description:
The NRMO9WH is the plain white sibling in Nostalgia's lineup, trading the retro styling for a cleaner modern look. It keeps the 800 watt output and 0.9 cubic foot cavity, and adds an LED digital display, a child lock and an easy-clean interior. It is the one to buy if you want the Nostalgia platform without the retro cabinet.

The easy-clean interior is a practical detail, since a smooth cavity wipes down faster than a textured one. Twelve pre-programmed settings, a delay timer and express cooking are shared with the retro model. The child lock gives it an edge over the plainer budget units in a family home.

Care is routine: wipe the cavity after spatter, rinse the tray and leave airflow room. White cabinets show stains more than black, so wipe the front promptly. If you want the least expensive honest 800 watt unit here, this is it. Compared with the retro model, you give up the styling and keep the same cooking hardware, so the savings are real. It is the sensible default for a college room, a basement kitchen or a first apartment where the microwave mostly reheats.
products.bestFor: Shoppers who want a basic white 800 W microwave with a child lock.
cons: White finish shows stains over time

buyingCriteria.explanation: An 800 watt oven cooks roughly a fifth slower than a 1000 watt model, so a two-minute label time becomes about two and a half. That is workable for reheating but noticeable for full plates and frozen meals. Package directions assume 1000 to 1200 watts, which means you add time and check often. The GE Profile makes up for this with a sensor, while the Nostalgia units leave the arithmetic to you. A useful habit is to write the adjusted times for your five most common foods on a card taped inside a cabinet door until they become second nature. Do not trust a package time blindly, and always start at the low end of the range.

A moisture sensor, as on the GE Profile, tracks steam and ends the cycle when food is hot. Fixed presets, as on the Nostalgia models, run a set time that assumes a standard portion. Sensors handle odd portions better, but covered dishes can fool them. At lower wattages, where timing is already unfamiliar, a sensor removes the most guesswork. Even so, stirring and resting remain the best way to avoid cold centers, because no sensor can see inside a dense bowl of pasta or rice. Treat sensor presets as a strong first guess and add ten seconds if the middle is still cool.

The GE Profile measures 1.1 cubic feet and the Nostalgia models 0.9, a gap that decides whether a wide dinner plate turns freely. Capacity is a weak guide, and tray width matters more, so measure your plates. A cavity that is too tight can also leave a dish scraping the wall as it rotates. Bring one of your regular plates and bowls to the measuring tape rather than trusting a cubic foot figure. Also remember that tall containers need ceiling clearance, which a shallow retro cabinet may not give.

The GE Profile and Nostalgia NRMO9WH both list a child lock, which blocks stray presses in a family kitchen. A lock does not make a microwave child-safe on its own, because hot food and steam remain a risk. Put the unit at a height children cannot reach and keep cords tidy. Teach older children to use the oven only with supervision and to let covered dishes stand before lifting the lid. Steam burns, not the appliance itself, cause most injuries around a microwave.

The Nostalgia retro cabinet is a design statement, while the NRMO9WH is plain white and the GE Profile stainless. Stainless shows fingerprints, white shows stains and a retro paint finish can chip. Choose the finish you will tolerate wiping, since the cooking performance is similar. A glossy retro paint finish looks sharp in the first year, yet it can chip where the door handle gets hand contact. Stainless hides scratches better than paint but needs a microfiber cloth for fingerprints.

The same GE Profile is sold in stainless, black and white, so confirm the model number before you buy. Third-party sellers sometimes list near-twins with different wattages. An 800 watt label on the box should match the spec sheet, since a mismatch changes cook times. Before you click buy, compare the output wattage on the listing with the rating label in the product photos. Sellers occasionally reuse one photo set across wattage variants, which is how buyers end up with a 700 watt unit instead of the 800 watt one they wanted.

howWeEvaluated.title: Wattage purity
howWeEvaluated.description: We kept only units that list 800 W as their output. Many 700 W and 900 W models appear in search results and were removed. That left three distinct machines, so the guide stays short instead of padding. Listings that repeat the same model in another color were treated as one machine. We also set aside imported units built for other voltages.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cooking aids
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared sensor logic with fixed presets. The GE Profile has a moisture sensor, while the Nostalgia models rely on twelve presets. Aids that reduce guesswork on a slower oven earned more credit. A long preset list was not treated as an advantage by itself, because fixed times ignore portion size. The sensor on the GE Profile counted for more than the extra eight presets on the Nostalgia models.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cavity and fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared capacity from the spec sheets. The GE Profile at 1.1 cu ft sits above the 0.9 cu ft Nostalgia units. Plate fit was weighted above volume. We also noted that a deeper cavity helps with tall bowls, which the shallower retro cabinet may not accept. Exterior width was checked so that a unit does not overwhelm a small counter.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety features
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked for child locks and control layouts. The GE Profile and NRMO9WH list a child lock, and the retro unit does not. Safety features rated higher in family settings. A lock is not a substitute for supervision, so it counted as a convenience rather than a guarantee. Door design and interior light were noted where the listing mentioned them.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership signals
howWeEvaluated.description: Reviews from owners gravitate toward touch pads and door latches as wear points in this price class. Easy-clean interiors earned credit, and finish variants were checked for model confusion. Standard one year coverage is typical, so we did not rank by warranty. Simplicity of design counted in favor of units with fewer electronic parts to fail.

cards.label: Sensor
cards.text: The GE Profile watches steam and ends the cycle when food is hot. It copes with changing portion sizes and is helpful at 800 W, where timing is unfamiliar. It can mislead on covered dishes.

cards.label: Presets
cards.text: The Nostalgia retro and NRMO9WH run twelve fixed-time presets. They are simple and predictable for standard foods. They do not adapt to portion size.

howToChoose.note: Pick the GE Profile if you reheat varied portions. Pick a Nostalgia model if you use standard foods and want the lowest cost.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A small kitchen needs a compact cabinet, quiet operation and a cavity that still takes a normal plate. A 0.9 cu ft body saves counter but limits dishes.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Nostalgia NRMO9WH is the leanest, and the GE Profile gives more room if your counter allows it. The retro Nostalgia unit makes the most visual impact.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You reheat varied portions and want the oven to judge time. The GE Profile earns its cost through sensor cooking and a bigger cavity.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You use the oven for drinks, snacks and standard frozen meals. The Nostalgia NRMO9WH gives the basics with a child lock.

maintenance.why: Baked-on splatter absorbs energy and can cause hot spots. A damp cloth while warm is easiest.
Grease on the tray smokes when heated. Dry it fully before placing it back.
A film of food residue stops the door from closing fully. Use mild soap and a soft cloth.
A fogged cavity can skew the GE Profile sensor reading. Leave the door open briefly to dry it.
Vents that get blocked trap heat and shorten magnetron life. Vacuum dust from the slots.

faq.q: Is an 800 watt microwave worth buying?
faq.a: It works for reheating and light cooking, but it is slower than the common 1000 watt class. If you can choose any wattage, 1000 watts is usually better. Choose 800 watts only when the cabinet, finish or price suits you. The speed gap versus 1000 watts shows up most on frozen meals and large bowls, and barely on a mug of coffee. A buyer who mainly reheats drinks and snacks will never notice it.

faq.q: How much longer do I need to cook at 800 watts?
faq.a: Plan on roughly a fifth more time than the label for a 1000 watt oven. A sensor model like the GE Profile reduces the guesswork. For others, check food early and add time in small steps. Stirring halfway through is worth more than another minute on the clock. Covering a dish loosely keeps moisture in and helps the slower heat reach the center.

faq.q: Why are there so few 800 watt microwaves?
faq.a: Most makers stick to 700, 900, 1000 and 1100 watt tiers. The 800 watt slot is thinly populated, so this guide covers only the distinct machines that really carry it. We did not pad it with near-wattage units. If a listing shows a different wattage in its title and its spec table, treat the spec table as the one to trust. Imported models built for 220 volt outlets are not suitable for a standard home.

faq.q: Is the GE Profile worth the higher cost?
faq.a: If you reheat varied portions, the sensor and larger cavity are worth it. If you only warm drinks and snacks, a Nostalgia unit is enough. It depends on how much you value automatic cooking. The larger 1.1 cubic foot cavity also helps with wide plates, which the 0.9 cubic foot Nostalgia models handle less comfortably. Households with several cooks will get more from the sensor than a single user with a fixed routine.

No. The Nostalgia retro uses a standard timer-and-power design, with styling as the main difference. The tradeoff is fixed presets and no sensor. Appearance is the reason to choose it. The cabinet is the same basic box underneath, so reliability depends on the same parts as any budget oven. If you plan to keep the unit in view, the finish matters more than a spec line.

faq.q: Are these microwaves safe around kids?
faq.a: A child lock blocks stray presses, as on the GE Profile and NRMO9WH. It does not remove the risk of hot food. Place the unit out of small children's reach. Let covered dishes stand for a moment before opening, since trapped steam can scald. Keep the door seal clean so the door closes fully.
